lines: “Oil is cheaper — so shouldn’t every fuel price fall?”

slides.title: Follow the barrel from production to consumer
lines: Crude supply recovery does not instantly restore every finished product.

slides.title: The refined products are not interchangeable
lines: Passenger mobility, seasonal blends and local demand.
Each product has its own inventory, trade flow, margin and demand cycle.

slides.title: Why a refinery outage changes the outcome
lines: The upstream barrel may be physically available and cheaper.
Conversion capacity, turnaround, product quality or transport can restrict diesel availability.
A product shortfall can coexist with ample crude inventories.

slides.title: A restriction travels through several markets
lines: Higher cracks may encourage runs where spare capacity exists — not as an unconditional law.

slides.title: Unit mismatches can create a fake margin
lines: Use price/volume units, crude grade, product quality, market location and month consistently.
Do not compare diesel dollars-per-gallon directly with crude dollars-per-barrel.

slides.title: A blend of gasoline and distillate economics
lines: Hypothetical barrel values. Actual refinery yields and costs differ.
A benchmark gross spread, not a universal refinery output recipe.

slides.title: Brent and WTI price different things
lines: Global seaborne benchmark influenced by international trade, quality, logistics and contract conventions.
US light-sweet crude benchmark with different location, delivery and regional dynamics.
Same-day front-month futures are not identical to delivered spot cargo margins.

slides.title: The four checks behind a real diesel story
lines: Are inventories scarce in the region that matters?
Are utilisation and product yields constrained?
Can arbitrage and shipping relieve the shortage?
Is the industrial/freight cycle changing consumption?

slides.title: Backwardation is a signal, not a price forecast
lines: Nearby product futures command a premium to deferred delivery — may reflect immediate scarcity/convenience value.
Deferred contracts exceed nearby prices — may reflect storage/financing and inventory conditions.
Do not infer the eventual future spot price directly from curve slope.

slides.title: A ship sighting is not a cargo delivery
lines: Some vessel location and movement signals, subject to coverage gaps, spoofing and delay.
Verified cargo volume, delivery completion, grade, contract terms, availability to refiners, or permanent normalisation.
Separate crude, refined products and LNG. Preserve timestamps and stale-data flags.

slides.title: How a diesel shortage can reach bond markets
lines: Transmission is conditional on demand, expectations and policy response.

slides.title: What could make the crude–diesel divergence disappear?
lines: Refinery restarts, exports resume, logistics unclog.
Freight, manufacturing or seasonal consumption eases.
Local premium fades while benchmark crude changes.
A headline is an opening hypothesis, not proof of the underlying cause.
